subtopics.name: Aging process and older adult health

questions.stem: According to Erikson, what is the main developmental task of adolescence?

rationale.correct: Erikson: trust (infant), autonomy (toddler), initiative (preschool), industry (school age), identity (adolescent), intimacy (young adult), generativity (middle adult), integrity (older adult).

perOption.a: Adolescents work to form a sense of self.
perOption.b: This is the task of infancy.
perOption.c: This is the task of school-age children.
perOption.d: This is the task of older adulthood.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old client enjoys talking about past accomplishments. Which intervention supports this client's developmental task?

options.text: Redirect the client to current events only
Suggest the client start a new career

rationale.correct: Older adults work toward integrity; reminiscence supports it.

perOption.a: Reviewing life supports integrity rather than despair.
perOption.b: This discourages a healthy developmental process.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Support ego integrity in older adults.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old mentors younger coworkers and volunteers in the community. Which developmental task does this reflect?

rationale.correct: Middle adulthood: generativity, contributing to others and the next generation.

perOption.a: Middle adults focus on guiding the next generation.
perOption.b: This is the task of young adulthood.
perOption.c: This is the task of adolescence.
perOption.d: This is the task of preschoolers.

questions.stem: Which findings are expected changes of normal aging? Select all that apply.

rationale.correct: Know normal aging versus findings that need evaluation, such as delirium or incontinence.

perOption.a: Collagen and elastin decrease with age.
perOption.c: Age-related hearing loss affects high frequencies.
perOption.d: This raises the risk of dehydration.
perOption.e: Acute confusion isn't normal aging and suggests delirium.
perOption.f: Bladder capacity falls, but incontinence isn't a normal part of aging.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: Which teaching approach is best for an older adult?

options.text: Short sessions at a slower pace, with large-print materials and time for questions
Long sessions with lots of information at once
Speaking quickly to keep the client's attention

rationale.correct: Adapt teaching to sensory and cognitive changes in older adults.

perOption.a: This accommodates changes in vision, hearing and processing speed.
perOption.d: Vision changes make this hard to read.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old pregnant client at 28 weeks asks which vaccine is recommended during each pregnancy. What is the nurse's response?

rationale.correct: In pregnancy: Tdap each pregnancy (27 to 36 weeks) and inactivated influenza; avoid live vaccines.

perOption.a: Tdap in each pregnancy passes pertussis antibodies to the newborn.
perOption.b: Live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy.
perOption.c: Live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy.
perOption.d: Tdap and inactivated influenza are recommended.

references: CDC/ACIP immunization schedules

questions.stem: Which client should not receive the MMR vaccine today?

options.text: A client with a mild cold
A client with an egg allergy

rationale.correct: Live vaccines (MMR, varicella, live intranasal influenza) are avoided in pregnancy and severe immunosuppression.

perOption.a: MMR is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy.
perOption.b: A mild illness isn't a contraindication.
perOption.d: Egg allergy isn't a contraindication to MMR.

options.text: Anaphylaxis after a previous dose of the same vaccine
Soreness at the site after the last dose

rationale.correct: True contraindications are uncommon; avoid missed opportunities to vaccinate.

perOption.a: A severe allergic reaction to a prior dose is a contraindication.

questions.stem: Which vaccines are usually given at a healthy child's 12-month visit?

rationale.correct: Know the key schedule points: hepatitis B at birth; DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV and rotavirus at 2, 4 and 6 months; MMR and varicella at 12 to 15 months.

perOption.a: The first doses of MMR and varicella are given at 12 to 15 months.
perOption.c: HPV is given at 9 to 12 years.
perOption.d: Tdap is given at 11 to 12 years.

references: CDC/ACIP immunization schedules

options.text: "The recombinant zoster vaccine is recommended at 50 and older, given as 2 doses."
"It's only for people who have had shingles."

rationale.correct: Recombinant zoster vaccine: 2 doses for adults 50 and older (and some younger immunocompromised adults).

perOption.a: Recombinant zoster vaccine is recommended for adults 50 and older.
perOption.b: It is recommended whether or not the person has had shingles.

questions.stem: For each infant milestone, indicate the age by which it usually appears.

rationale.correct: Use milestones to screen development and refer when they are delayed.

perOption.r1:c1: The social smile appears at about 2 months.
perOption.r2:c2: Infants usually sit unsupported by 6 to 8 months.
perOption.r2:c3: This is a little late as the expected age.
perOption.r3:c3: The pincer grasp develops around 9 to 10 months.
perOption.r4:c3: This is early for most infants.
perOption.r4:c4: Independent walking usually starts at 12 to 15 months.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: An infant weighed 3.5 kg at birth. About what weight should the nurse expect at 12 months?

rationale.correct: Birth weight doubles by about 5 to 6 months and triples by 12 months.

perOption.a: Birth weight usually triples by 12 months.
perOption.b: Birth weight doubles by about 5 to 6 months.

questions.stem: A parent asks how to handle a 2-year-old's temper tantrums. What is the best advice?

options.text: "Keep your child safe and ignore the tantrum, then praise calm behavior."
"Spank your child to stop the behavior."

rationale.correct: Toddlers: autonomy versus shame; use consistent limits, simple choices and ignoring when safe.

perOption.a: Ignoring tantrums while ensuring safety reduces them; toddlers are seeking autonomy.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

perOption.b: Preschoolers have limited time concepts; long lead times raise anxiety.

questions.stem: The nurse is doing a health history with a 15-year-old who came with a parent. What is the best approach?

options.text: Interview the adolescent alone for part of the visit, explaining confidentiality and its limits
Ask the parent to answer all the questions
Tell the teen that everything will be shared with the parent

rationale.correct: Adolescents: privacy, confidentiality (with its limits) and screening for risk behaviors (HEEADSSS).

perOption.a: Privacy encourages honest disclosure about risk behaviors.

options.text: "Keep it rear-facing as long as possible, until your child reaches the seat's height or weight limit."

rationale.correct: Rear-facing car seats protect the head and neck; keep children rear-facing to the seat's limits.

perOption.a: Rear-facing is safest; current guidance is to stay rear-facing to the seat's limits.

questions.stem: Which statement by a new parent shows correct understanding of safe sleep?

options.text: "I'll put my baby on her back on a firm mattress with no blankets or bumpers."
"I'll put my baby on her stomach so she won't choke."
"She'll sleep in my bed every night."

rationale.correct: Safe sleep: back to sleep, firm flat surface, empty crib, room-sharing without bed-sharing.

perOption.a: This reduces the risk of SIDS and suffocation.
perOption.d: Bed-sharing increases risk; room-sharing is recommended.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: Which child is at highest risk for lead poisoning?

options.text: A 2-year-old living in a house built in 1950 with peeling paint
A 10-year-old living in a new apartment
A 6-month-old who is exclusively breastfed in a new home

rationale.correct: Lead risk: homes built before 1978, hand-to-mouth behavior and certain imported products; screen high-risk toddlers.

perOption.a: Older homes may have lead paint; toddlers put things in their mouths.
